title: Teaching with ChatGPT as a Linguistically Responsive Tool for Multilingual Learners
extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers of K–12 multilingual learners in U.S. public schools are using ChatGPT and related AI tools to support language and literacy instruction. The study is motivated by concerns that multilingual learners are often taught through monolingual, deficit-oriented practices, and asks whether generative AI can be used in more linguistically responsive ways.

The author analyzes classroom observations and post-observation interviews from 42 in-service teachers participating in a professional development course focused on culturally and linguistically responsive pedagogy. The teachers worked across pre-K through 12th grade in multiple contexts, including general education, ESL, dual-language bilingual education, Spanish immersion, special education, science, math, and ELA. Instances of ChatGPT use were identified in 8 observations.

The findings show that teachers mainly used ChatGPT to facilitate communication (for example, translating text, transcribing student speech, and generating subtitles) and to differentiate content (for example, adjusting reading levels or creating exemplar texts). In some secondary classrooms, teachers also scaffolded students’ prompting skills and used ChatGPT’s image-generation capabilities for multimodal literacy activities. The author concludes that these uses align most clearly with the affordances, production, and co-labor dimensions of translanguaging pedagogy, but that assessment and reflection were notably absent. The paper argues that generative AI has promise for supporting multilingual learners’ access and agency, while also calling for more critical, explicit, and ethical guidance around its use.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot and LLM-based assistant for text generation, translation, prompting, and other language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a linguistically responsive tool used by K-12 teachers of multilingual learners to facilitate communication, differentiate content, support prompting, and enable multimodal literacy experimentation.

findings.finding_summary: Across observations and interviews with 42 in-service teachers, ChatGPT was used to translate texts, transcribe student speech, create subtitles, differentiate reading levels, and generate exemplar texts for multilingual learners. The study reports these practices as supporting comprehension, access to content, writing support, and multilingual/multimodal participation, but it does not report quantitative effect sizes.
findings.measure: Classroom instructional uses observed in field notes and post-observation interviews; qualitative evidence of support for comprehension, access, and participation
findings.sample_size: n=42 teachers observed; ChatGPT documented in 8 observations

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used ChatGPT to facilitate communication across languages by translating vocabulary and passages, translating/transcribing student oral language, and helping students draft or revise prompts and writing in preferred languages. The paper characterizes these uses as improving access to language and content for multilingual learners, but no numerical effects are reported.
findings.measure: Observed teacher practices related to translation, transcription, and language support
findings.sample_size: n=42 teachers observed; ChatGPT documented in 8 observations

findings.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT aligned with translanguaging dimensions of affordances, production, and co-labor, but not assessment or reflection. It also notes limitations such as lack of resources to verify translation quality and concerns about overreliance, bias, and standard-language norms.
findings.measure: Qualitative alignment with translanguaging framework dimensions; documented limitations and gaps
findings.sample_size: n=42 teachers observed; ChatGPT documented in 8 observations

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods classroom observation and interview study, so it does not meet blue/green experimental evidence standards. The paper provides structured empirical documentation of use cases, but no causal estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports potentially meaningful instructional benefits for multilingual learners, but those benefits are described qualitatively without effect sizes or outcome measures. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.
